'''Paul Grobstein''' (March 21, 1946 – June 28, 2011) was an American neurobiologist who studied the development and organization of nervous systems.  In addition to his work in neurobiology, Grobstein had  a long-term interest in understanding people's behavior.

==Early life==
Paul was born on March 21, 1946, in [[Los Angeles]] to [[doi:10.1007/s10897-012-9503-0|Rose Gruver Grobstein]] and [[Clifford Grobstein]]. Clifford Grobstein, an American biologist and cancer researcher, was a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="NYTimes">{{cite news|last1=Grady |first1=Denise |title=Clifford Grobstein, 82, Biologist Who Applied Ethics to Research |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/09/13/us/clifford-grobstein-82-biologist-who-applied-ethics-to-research.html |access-date=29 May 2023 |work=New York Times |date=13 September 1998}}</ref> Rose Grobstein, an American social worker, was a pioneer and “founding mother” in the field of [[genetic counseling]].<ref name="PeninsulaTimes">{{cite news |title=Separating mother, child damages relationship |issue=11 |publisher=The Peninsula Times Tribute |date=11 May 1972}}</ref> Paul grew up with one younger sister, Joan Grobstein. In 1950 the family lived in [[Bethesda, Maryland]].<ref name=USCensus>{{cite United States census | url =https://1950census.archives.gov/ | title = 1950 United States Federal Census | year =1950 | location = | roll =2547 | page = 11| line = 4| enumdist =16–50 | filmnum = | nafilm = | accessdate = 29 May 2023}}</ref> Later they moved to [[Palo Alto, California]] where Clifford was on the [[Stanford University]] faculty and Paul attended [[Palo Alto High School]].

==Education and career==
Grobstein received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in biology from [[Harvard University]] in 1969 and his [[Master of Arts]] and [[PhD]] in biology from [[Stanford University]] in 1970 and 1973. After postdoctoral fellowships at [[Johns Hopkins University]] and Stanford University, Grobstein joined the faculty of the [[University of Chicago]] in 1974 as an assistant professor; he left Chicago in 1985 as an associate professor. Grobstein spent the rest of his academic career at [[Bryn Mawr College]] where he joined the biology department as chair and professor in 1986. In 1988 he was awarded the Eleanor A. Bliss Professorship at Bryn Mawr, and he founded the Summer Institutes for K-12 Teachers in 1990 which brought hundreds of local educators to campus to consider new ways of teaching science and math. In 2000 he founded and was director of the Center for Science in Society.<ref name=stanfordobit>{{cite web|title=Obituaries-November/December 2011|date=November 2011 |url=https://stanfordmag.org/contents/obituaries-3746|publisher=Stanford University|access-date=27 May 2023}}</ref><ref name=carleton>{{cite web|title=Bryn Mawr College Summer Institutes for K-12 Teachers|url=https://serc.carleton.edu/teacherprep/programs/BMC-SumInst.html|publisher=Science Education Resource Center at Carleton University|access-date=27 May 2023}}</ref>  Grobstein was associate editor of the Journal of Research Practice from 2005 to 2011.<ref name="JRP">{{cite journal |last1=Dalke |first1=Anne |title=Paul Grobstein (Associate Editor, JRP, 2005–2011) |journal=Journal of Research Practice |date=11 March 2011 |volume=7 |issue=1 |page=1}}</ref>

==Research and innovation==
His laboratory research concentrated on the development and organization of the nervous systems of various animals including crayfish, rabbits, leeches, and significantly frogs, where the focus of his work was "the nature of spatial representations and the origins, organization, regulation, and significance of unpredictability in neuronal function and behavior".<ref name=serendipbio>{{cite web|title=Paul Grobstein Serendip co-founder|url=https://serendipstudio.org/local/grobstein.html| access-date=27 May 2023}}</ref> In addition to his work in neurobiology Grobstein had  a long-term interest in understanding people's behavior. In 1994, together with Deepak Kumar, Professor of Computer Science at Bryn Mawr College, and Ann Dixon, Bryn Mawr College alumna, he created Serendip, an intellectual community dedicated to gathering people together for the exploration of science. Serendip was the first website on the Bryn Mawr campus and originally Serendip hosted the Bryn Mawr College website. In 2005 the site consisted of over 20,000 pages and averaged 20,000 unique visitors a day. The site has a section that encourages interactive educational experiences and another that promotes online interactive discussions. There are many other sections on the site including a more recent addition that provides resources for teaching about the coronavirus.<ref>{{cite web | title=Serendip's 10th Anniversary: An Invitation to an Intellectual Playground | website=Serendip Studio's One World | date=2001-09-11 | url=https://serendipstudio.org/serendip/alumbulletin2005.html | ref={{sfnref | Serendip Studio's One World | 2001}} | access-date=2023-06-01}}</ref><ref name="DixonSerendip">{{cite journal |last1=Dixon |first1=Ann |title=Serendip |journal=Bryn Mawr Alumnae Bulletin |date=November 2005 |pages=14–19}}</ref>

==Recognition==
Grobstein was an [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] Fellow from 1976 to 1980.<ref name =sloan>{{cite web|url=https://sloan.org/fellows-database|title=Fellows Database|publisher=Alfred P. Sloan Foundation|access-date=1 June 2023}}</ref> Grobstein received the Rosalyn R. Schwartz Teaching Award for teaching excellence and campus leadership at Bryn Mawr in 1988.<ref name=stanfordobit /> In that same year he was appointed to the Eleanor A. Bliss Professorship.<ref name=brynmawr>{{cite web|title=Bryn Mawr Biology Faculty|website=Bryn Mawr College|url=http://www.brynmawr.edu/Adm/academic/biologyfaculty.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001020212043/http://www.brynmawr.edu/Adm/academic/biologyfaculty.html|archive-date=20 October 2000}}</ref>  In 2000 he was named founding director of the Center for Science in Society at Bryn Mawr.  To honor Grobstein after his death in 2011 Bryn Mawr College established the Paul Grobstein Memorial Fund.<ref name=inquirerobit>{{cite web|title=Paul Grobstein Obituary|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/inquirer/name/paul-grobstein-obituary?id=10055425|publisher=Philadelphia Inquirer|access-date=28 May 2023}}</ref>
